option_assessments.label: A
option_assessments.truth: FALSE for usual Kotlin reading of T as a generic type parameter: nullability is statically distinguished, and T? is not merely a runtime distinction.
option_assessments.refutation: Unbounded T has upper bound Any? and can be nullable; the compiler enforces nullability distinctions.
option_assessments.ansc: Addresses how T and T? differ, so it covers the visible null-safety question despite being false.
option_assessments.sfpl: Abstract generic phrasing; similar compact declarative form to D, with no uniquely complete multi-part treatment.
option_assessments.ru: Clear, though “лишь в рантайме” is technical colloquialism.

option_assessments.label: B
option_assessments.truth: FALSE: nullable receivers generally require safe call, explicit check/smart cast, or !!; direct unrestricted member access is not allowed.
option_assessments.refutation: Compiler rejects direct member access on nullable receiver in ordinary member calls.
option_assessments.ansc: Directly addresses null-safety mechanism and is complete as a broad claim, although false.
option_assessments.sfpl: One concise declarative assertion, comparable surface form to other choices.
option_assessments.ru: Understandable; “свободно обращаться” and quoted “без” are slightly awkward but clear.

option_assessments.label: C
option_assessments.truth: FALSE: platform types have relaxed checks, not guaranteed compiler nullability validation; null can cause runtime failure.
option_assessments.refutation: Java declarations without recognized nullability info may be platform types; recognized annotations instead yield nullable/non-null types.
option_assessments.ansc: Covers Java interop as one aspect of null-safety, though narrower than full language mechanism.
option_assessments.sfpl: Specific technical claim with one sentence like peers; truth is separate from form.
option_assessments.ru: Readable; “приходят с ... проверкой” is a little unnatural.

option_assessments.label: D
option_assessments.truth: FALSE as a universal generic claim. True for concrete non-null T such as String, but unbounded generic T can be nullable because upper bound is Any?.
option_assessments.refutation: The theory itself says not every T is non-null; <T : Any> is needed to exclude nullable arguments. The visible item states no such bound.
option_assessments.ansc: Addresses null/non-null distinction directly and is complete for the visible broad question, despite false universal wording.
option_assessments.sfpl: Only option that explains nullability using paired types and compiler guarantee; potentially more complete/definitional than others, a form/completeness imbalance.
option_assessments.ru: Clear and concise; “тип-вопрос” is awkward/unclear technical wording.

section_assessments.assessment: Correct distinguishes T and T? at compile time, but generic T is not inherently non-null; with unconstrained upper bound Any? it may be nullable.
Plausible confusion about runtime representation; does not fully capture compile-time nullability.
Valid consequence of the false runtime-only claim, though narrow and does not explain type distinctions.
Correct broad principle: nullability belongs to type system.
Correct: nullable values cannot generally be accessed without null handling; nullable-receiver extensions are an exception omitted by this simplification.
Correct examples of safe call or explicit check; not exhaustive (smart cast, !! also exist).
Partly wrong: platform types are not guaranteed statically checked for nullability; Java annotations can produce actual nullable/non-null types.
Plausible confusion but overgeneralizes all Java types as safe.
Plausible consequence of guaranteed checks, though NPE can occur from other causes; its “through interop” scope makes it a reasonable local inference.
False/overbroad: NPE through interop can occur, but also via !!, explicit throw, initialization issues; platform types are not the only route.
Correct for concrete T=String, but literally universal T is false: unbounded T has upper bound Any? and may accept nullable types; requires unstated non-null bound/concrete type.
Good concrete String/String? example that demonstrates Kotlin type distinction; it does not prove all generic T excludes null.
Relevant but generic and circular; does not add application guidance.
Accurate but incomplete description: not all Java types become platform types; recognized annotations map to nullable/non-null types.
Mixed: operators are idiomatic; calling !! a code smell is a style judgment, not a universal language fact.

axes.SEMANTICS: FAIL: D is false for generic T without a visible non-null bound. A also misstates compile-time distinction as runtime-only; B and C are false as phrased.
axes.ANSC: All four address a relevant part of the broad visible question; D is the most direct paired-type account, but factual falsity is scored separately.
axes.SFPL: FAIL: D alone gives a paired type distinction plus compiler behavior, making it comparatively complete; truth does not itself count as form.
axes.RU: MIXED: generally understandable, with awkward “тип-вопрос” (D) and somewhat unnatural phrasing in C/B.
axes.FACTS: Official Kotlin docs: nullable distinction is type-system enforced; unbounded generic upper bound is Any?; Java platform types have relaxed checks and recognized nullability annotations map to Kotlin nullable/non-null types; NPE may also arise from !!, explicit throw, initialization.
axes.SECTIONS: Mixed: A.what_actually ignores generic T bounds; C.how_it_should_be overgeneralizes NPE origin; D.explanation universalizes generic T; D.example supports concrete String distinction only; D.edge_cases misses annotated Java types.
axes.LINKAGE: D aligns to basic String/String? theory, but universal T wording conflicts with the provided generic caveat. A explicitly references T yet has unsupported runtime-only claim.

current_theory: Provided Q4 theory states nullability is a static type-system feature; concrete String vs String? differ, but unbounded T is not necessarily non-null (upper bound Any?); <T : Any> excludes nullable arguments. Java references without recognized nullability info may become platform types with relaxed checks; annotated Java types map to nullable/non-null Kotlin types. NPE can also result from !!, explicit throw, initialization errors.
limits: D is evaluated literally as an unbounded generic T because no bound is stated visibly; if T was intended to mean a concrete non-null type, that condition is unstated.
Theories and sections are assessed from supplied exact payload; no corpus edits or registry inspection.
No change made to the blind A record; its earlier D choice differs from this source-based review because the generic upper-bound caveat makes D non-universal.
